name: Rocky Mountain National Park
blurb: Elk, willow and aspen, and a mountain food web in a warming climate.

tip.title: Shrink the snowpack
tip.text: Snowmelt waters meadows and streams. Cut Snowpack & snowmelt by 60% and watch willows and sedges, then the elk, moose and beaver that eat them.

sources.title: NPS: Mammals of Rocky Mountain National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Willows
nodes.desc: Streamside shrubs of the montane valleys. The park page says elk overgrazing has damaged riparian areas, so some wetlands are fenced to let willows recover.

nodes.name: Quaking aspen
nodes.desc: A leafy tree of moister montane slopes. Elk like its spring sprouts, and groves have declined in places where elk are numerous.

nodes.name: Lodgepole pine
nodes.desc: A conifer that recolonizes old burn areas in the subalpine zone. It is a host of the mountain pine beetle.

nodes.name: Grasses & sedges
nodes.desc: Meadow and tundra grasses and sedges. Year-round food for elk, and pikas and marmots eat them too.

nodes.name: Alpine tundra plants
nodes.desc: Low cushion plants, such as moss campion, make up the tundra vegetation, which covers over a third of the park. Recovery from trampling takes centuries.

nodes.name: Moose
nodes.desc: Reintroduced to the park in 1978 and now common, especially on the west side. Browses willow and birch shoots.

nodes.name: North American beaver
nodes.desc: A montane mammal that cuts woody stems for food and dams. Willow and aspen are typical foods.

nodes.name: Elk
nodes.desc: Mostly a grazer that also browses. With wolves absent, the park culls some elk each winter and fences some wetlands from them.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: A browsing deer and the main prey of the park's mountain lions, per the park page.

nodes.name: Mountain pine beetle
nodes.desc: A bark beetle that kills conifers. The park page says warmer winters let it survive and reproduce faster, raising tree mortality.

nodes.name: American pika
nodes.desc: A small tundra and talus herbivore that stores dried plants as haypiles. It overheats in warm weather and relies on cool rock crevices.

nodes.name: Yellow-bellied marmot
nodes.desc: A burrowing herbivore of meadows and rock slopes, listed among the park's mammals.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A very well-recorded park bird that eats carrion, seeds, berries and small animals.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that is uncommon in the park (the park page gives only a few dozen). Eats plants, calves and carrion, and often visits cougar kills.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: A widespread predator. Elk page notes coyotes mostly take calves, and pikas count coyotes among their predators.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: A common soaring raptor of open country that hunts small mammals and birds.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: The park's top predator, taking mostly mule deer, per the park page. Wikipedia lists elk and moose among cougar prey elsewhere.

nodes.name: Snowpack & snowmelt
nodes.desc: Winter snow feeds meadows and streams through the dry summer. The park page says warming brings earlier melt, drier summers and a longer fire season.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Low-severity fire helps keep the forest in balance. The 2012 Fern Lake Fire burned nearly 3,500 acres after long fire-free years.

nodes.name: Soil nutrients
nodes.desc: Thin mountain soils recycled from dead plants and animals feed forest, meadow and tundra plants.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, needles, plants and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.
